title: Center for Brooklyn History — Lenape and Montaukett Records
summary: This Brooklyn Heights research library holds Jasper Danckaerts’ journal of 1679–1680, one of the most detailed eyewitness accounts of Lenape life in Brooklyn, and the Proprietors of Montauk records, including Montaukett land receipts and Arthur Benson’s papers.

why_this_matters: Much of what is known about Lenape life in seventeenth-century Brooklyn, and about the loss of Montaukett land, survives in these Brooklyn Heights collections.
introduction_title: Records of Native Brooklyn and Montauk
introduction_content:
The Center for Brooklyn History, at 128 Pierrepont Street, keeps records that put Native people at the center of Brooklyn and Long Island history. They include the original Dutch-language journals of Jasper Danckaerts and Peter Sluyter from their travels of 1679–1681.[1]

Henry C. Murphy, a founder of the Long Island Historical Society, later the Brooklyn Historical Society, brought the journal to light.[3] The society’s records list the manuscript as purchased from Murphy in 1884.[1]
history_content:
A traveler’s view of Lenape Brooklyn

On September 29, 1679, Danckaerts walked through Breukelen to Gowanus. His host served venison he had bought from Native people for seawant, or wampum, and roasted Gowanus oysters, some “not less than a foot long.” The next day, at Najack near today’s Fort Hamilton, he found seven or eight families, about twenty people, living in a bark-covered house about sixty feet long beside their maize fields. They paid Jacques Cortelyou twenty bushels of maize a year to stay on a corner of land he had bought from them.[2]

New World Encounters, 1986

In 1986 the Brooklyn Historical Society’s exhibition New World Encounters drew on newly retranslated parts of the journal, including pages the first English edition had left out. Robert S. Grumet’s catalog traced how Brooklyn’s Lenape named themselves by home place, and where families went after the last Brooklyn tract was sold in 1684. It also described Brooklyn’s Native community as the largest in the greater New York area.[3]

Montauk records in Brooklyn

The center also holds the Proprietors of Montauk collection: Supreme Court records, Indian land receipts and the papers of Arthur Benson, the Brooklyn businessman who bought the proprietors’ Montauk holdings at auction in 1879.[4] Those papers document the long struggle over Montaukett land. See the Montauk Auction Landscape.
whereintheworld_content: The green dot marks the Center for Brooklyn History at 128 Pierrepont Street in Brooklyn Heights.[5] Danckaerts’ drawings are cataloged separately as prints and drawings.[1] Nearby, Marechkawick and Ihpetonga carry older names for this part of Brooklyn.
